facts.says: My shoulder's been bugging me for years from the job, so I pop ibuprofen most days, maybe 2-3 pills.

facts.says: My dad had high blood pressure too, he passed from a stroke at 68. My mom's got the sugar diabetes.

facts.chart: Former smoker, quit 6 years ago, previously 1 pack/day for 15 years.

facts.chart: Reports increased stress related to reduced work hours and finances.
facts.says: Honestly, with the hours cut, money's been stressful. It's on my mind a lot.

facts.chart: Denies leg or ankle swelling.

facts.chart: Reports waking twice nightly to urinate, which disrupts sleep in addition to snoring.
facts.says: I get up maybe twice a night to use the bathroom, on top of everything else.

facts.chart: Reports occasional dull morning headaches a few times a week.
facts.says: Some mornings I wake up with a dull headache, happens a few times a week.

facts.chart: No history of diabetes, kidney disease, or heart disease; prior labs normal.
facts.says: No, I don't have diabetes or kidney problems, my doctor said my labs were all fine a few months back.

facts.chart: No known drug allergies.
facts.says: No allergies to medicines that I know of.

facts.chart: Reports taking lisinopril consistently without missed doses, unlike amlodipine.
facts.says: The lisinopril one I never skip, it's the other one I've been stretching.

facts.chart: No prior surgeries.

facts.chart: Chronic right shoulder pain for 5 years, attributed to repetitive steering motion; no recent injury or acute change.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he takes both blood pressure medications every day without missing doses.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows amlodipine 5mg (90-day supply) was last filled 10 weeks ago, meaning it should have run out about 4 weeks ago with no refill since; lisinopril refill is on time.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often overestimates actual medication-taking; refill history is an objective adherence check, and uncovering a cost-related nonadherence barrier (rather than assuming simple forgetfulness) changes the management plan - here, addressing copay/access matters more than adding a new drug.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient discloses nearly falling asleep at a red light while driving the bus but asks that this not create trouble for him, implying he has not reported any sleep problem to anyone official.
mismatches.recordEvidence: CDL medical certificate record (a13) shows a routine renewal 8 months ago with no mention of any sleep-related condition or restriction on file, despite the high STOP-BANG score (a9) now indicating high risk for a condition that could affect fitness to safely operate a commercial vehicle.
mismatches.teachingPoint: When a patient's commercial driving safety may be at risk from a likely medical condition (suspected OSA), the clinician must balance patient confidentiality and trust with public safety obligations - this requires careful counseling about voluntary reporting/evaluation rather than silence, and referral for sleep study and DOT guidance, while recognizing scope: the family medicine resident refers rather than independently adjudicating fitness to drive.

objectives.text: Elicit true medication-taking patterns (vs. stated adherence) and identify cost as an access barrier, using refill history as objective evidence.
Recognize resistant/uncontrolled hypertension and identify contributing factors beyond adherence (NSAID use, decongestant use, diet, obesity).
Screen for obstructive sleep apnea using validated tools and recognize red-flag symptoms (witnessed apneas, near-miss drowsy driving event) that affect both health and commercial driving safety.
Navigate the tension between patient confidentiality/trust and the clinician's responsibility regarding commercial driving safety when a reluctant patient discloses a safety-relevant symptom.

Formulate an appropriately scoped family medicine plan: address adherence/cost barriers, counsel on NSAID/decongestant contribution to BP, refer for sleep study, and determine need for in-person visit or specialist referral rather than overreaching role boundaries. Note that fitness-to-drive certification itself is outside family medicine scope; the resident should rely on patient-reported CDL status and counsel on voluntary disclosure rather than independently pulling or adjudicating DOT records.
Interpret relevant chronic disease monitoring labs (BMP, lipids, A1c, urine albumin) in the context of hypertension follow-up.

profile.summary: "A 52-year-old bus driver with hypertension returns for a telehealth follow-up with elevated home BP readings despite being on amlodipine and lisinopril. The case teaches residents to uncover cost-related medication nonadherence, identify NSAID/decongestant contributors to poor BP control, screen for obstructive sleep apnea, and navigate the sensitive intersection of a commercial driver's safety-sensitive symptoms with patient trust and appropriate referral."
profile.title: "Uncontrolled Hypertension in a Bus Driver: Adherence Barriers and a Hidden Sleep Apnea Risk"
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home at his kitchen table in Cleveland, Ohio

answerKey.primaryProblem: Uncontrolled/resistant hypertension in the setting of partial medication nonadherence (cost-related), concurrent NSAID and decongestant use, and newly identified high risk for obstructive sleep apnea.
differential: Medication nonadherence (cost-related) as primary driver of poor BP control
NSAID-induced sodium retention/vasoconstriction contributing to elevated BP
Undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnea causing or worsening hypertension
True resistant hypertension requiring further antihypertensive titration once adherence/contributors addressed
Secondary hypertension (e.g., renal, endocrine) - less likely given normal BMP, no other red flags, but to be reconsidered if BP remains uncontrolled after addressing above
keyFindings: Home BP log averaging 156/96 over 3 weeks with correct cuff technique confirmed on camera
Pharmacy refill history reveals amlodipine stretched (last filled 10 weeks ago for a 90-day supply) despite patient's belief that he takes it daily; lisinopril refilled on time
Near-daily OTC ibuprofen use for chronic shoulder pain and frequent pseudoephedrine use for allergies, both of which can raise blood pressure

Positive STOP-BANG (6/8: snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, high BP, age >50, male sex) and Epworth (14/24) screens indicating high risk for obstructive sleep apnea, with witnessed apneas and a near-miss drowsy-driving event at a red light
Patient has not disclosed sleep symptoms or the near-miss driving event to anyone, including his DOT medical examiner, and is anxious about his CDL status
Basic metabolic panel, lipid panel, A1c, and urine albumin/creatinine all normal/stable, lowering likelihood of secondary hypertension or early renal injury at this time
plan: Address cost-related nonadherence directly and non-judgmentally: discuss copay assistance programs, generic/mail-order options, or switching to a formulary-preferred agent; coordinate with pharmacy/social work as needed

Counsel on reducing or substituting NSAID use for shoulder pain (e.g., topical NSAIDs, acetaminophen, non-pharmacologic measures) and limiting pseudoephedrine; discuss alternative allergy management (non-sympathomimetic antihistamine or saline rinses)

Order outpatient referral for diagnostic sleep study given high-risk OSA screen; explain rationale and reassure that evaluation and treatment (e.g., CPAP) are the path to protecting both his health and his ability to keep working safely

Counsel patient on voluntary disclosure to his DOT medical examiner per FMCSA guidance regarding the near-miss drowsy-driving event and suspected OSA; clarify that evaluation and treatment, not the diagnosis itself, determine certification outcome, and that the clinician cannot keep this safety-relevant information fully confidential if it poses an ongoing public safety risk - frame as collaborative next step rather than punitive

Recheck BP in 2-4 weeks once adherence and contributing OTC medication use are addressed before escalating antihypertensive regimen; defer any medication dose change until true adherence and reversible contributors are addressed, consistent with primary care scope
Reinforce home BP monitoring technique and recommend validating/recalibrating the home cuff against a clinic reading
Continue routine preventive monitoring (lipids, A1c, renal function) at next scheduled interval; no urgent escalation needed given reassuring labs

This visit remains within family medicine scope: refer to sleep medicine for formal testing/CPAP titration and rely on patient-reported CDL status rather than independently pulling or adjudicating DOT certification records; do not unilaterally report to DOT - counsel patient toward appropriate voluntary disclosure/process
redFlags: Witnessed breathing pauses during sleep and a near-miss drowsy-driving incident while operating a commercial vehicle warrant urgent attention given public safety implications
Severely uncontrolled BP readings (>180/120) would require same-day evaluation - not present here but should prompt escalation if seen
Significant unexplained weight gain, edema, or rising creatinine would raise concern for secondary causes or target-organ damage and need prompt work-up
educationPoints: Objective adherence data (refill history) often reveals gaps that patients are unaware of or reluctant to volunteer; approach discrepancies with curiosity and without judgment to uncover underlying barriers like cost
Common over-the-counter medications (NSAIDs, decongestants) are frequently overlooked contributors to poor blood pressure control and should be routinely screened for in hypertension follow-up

Validated screening tools (STOP-BANG, Epworth) are efficient, remote-feasible ways to risk-stratify for obstructive sleep apnea in primary care; STOP-BANG scoring should correctly credit all met criteria including age >50

Clinicians caring for commercial drivers must understand the balance between patient confidentiality and public safety obligations, and should know the general framework for voluntary disclosure to DOT medical examiners rather than acting unilaterally

Resistant hypertension work-up should first exclude pseudo-resistance (adherence, white-coat effect, improper technique, interfering substances) before adding medications or pursuing secondary hypertension work-up

Family medicine residents typically do not have independent access to or authority over DOT/CDL certification records; fitness-to-drive determinations and record review are outside primary care telehealth scope and should rely on patient report plus appropriate referral
